title: Dungeons & Dragons: Adventure Begins - an Introduction to Board Games and RPGs
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AO1WNfgIgiE

Daniel (@dungeondive) frames this one around gaming literacy — the idea that, like reading, each mechanism you learn opens the door to more games, and that too few designers think about the other side of that equation: how a game teaches. It is why he praises *Gloomhaven: Jaws of the Lion*'s onboarding despite disliking Gloomhaven, and why he was hard on *Aftermath*.

*Adventure Begins* is Hasbro's twenty-odd-dollar cooperative entry point, and its best ideas are in character creation. You slot a character into a tray, choose male or female art, then pick a personality — the Fixer, the Gambler, the Enforcer, the Genius — each a handful of keyword traits plus a small power. Then a backpack of items with no mechanical function at all: pure story seeds. Pick a boss (kraken, green dragon, beholder, fire giant), chain the tiles, and the DM deck passes player to player each turn. Straight moves draw encounters; optional side spaces offer enemies for gold and items at the cost of damage.

His reservation is where it falls short: encounters ask players to describe a plan, then resolve it on a flat d20 roll no plan can improve. Good art, good components, right audience — parents and newcomers, not gamers.

----

Games that teach games: what put the hobby in front of someone you know, and did it actually take?
